Let <MATH_0001> be a morphism of schemes.
Let <MATH_0002>. Assume that
<STRUCT_0001>
<STRUCT_0002> <MATH_0003> is locally of finite type, and
<STRUCT_0003> <MATH_0004> is a finite set.
<STRUCT_0004>
Then <MATH_0005> is a finite discrete topological space, and
<MATH_0006> is quasi-finite at each point of <MATH_0007> lying over <MATH_0008>.

Suppose <MATH_0001> is a scheme which (a) is locally of finite type
over a field <MATH_0002>, and (b) has finitely many points. Then
Lemma <REF_0001> shows <MATH_0003> is a
Jacobson scheme. A finite Jacobson space is discrete, see
Topology, Lemma <REF_0002>.
Apply this remark to the fibre <MATH_0004> which is locally of finite type over
<MATH_0005> to see the first statement. Finally, apply
Lemma <REF_0003> to see the second.

<LOCKED_0001>
Let <MATH_0001> be a morphism of schemes.
Assume <MATH_0002> is locally of finite type.
Then the following are equivalent
<STRUCT_0001>
<STRUCT_0002> <MATH_0003> is locally quasi-finite,
<STRUCT_0003> for every <MATH_0004> the fibre <MATH_0005> is a discrete topological space, and
<STRUCT_0004> for every morphism <MATH_0006> where <MATH_0007> is a field
the base change <MATH_0008> has an underlying discrete topological space.
<STRUCT_0005>

It is immediate that (3) implies (2).
Lemma <REF_0001>
shows that (2) is equivalent to (1).
Assume (2) and let <MATH_0001> be as in (3).
Denote <MATH_0002> the image  of <MATH_0003>.
Then <MATH_0004> is the base change of <MATH_0005> via
<MATH_0006>. Hence every
point of <MATH_0007> is closed by
Lemma <REF_0002>.
As <MATH_0008> is locally of finite type (by
Lemma <REF_0003>),
we may apply
Lemma <REF_0004>
to conclude that every point of <MATH_0009> is isolated, i.e., <MATH_0010> has
a discrete underlying topological space.
